utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like the appearances, please, on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I would like to turn now to the Defence attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now turning toward the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Rodney Dixon, and Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to welcome all the parties and people present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the representatives of the Defence team and the accused, as well as all the staff members and interpreters working in this courtroom this afternoon. We shall resume our court proceedings this afternoon after an interval which was due to the fact or related to Article 98 bis, legal break. Now, before Giving the floor to the Defence for its opening statement, I would like to turn to the Prosecution to say the following. The Trial Chamber is asking the Prosecution whether it intends to reply to the response made by the Defence which was filed on the 15th of October i.e., last Friday, insofar as the Trial Chamber is providing a posteriori, with hindsight, authorisation to the Defence to respond. As you know, given certification of appeal, which is required, we were -- the request -- a motion was sent to the Trial Chamber, and we replied. Last Friday, the Defence has filed a new motion whilst asking that authorisation be granted. This authorisation has been granted with hindsight, given the deadlines we were facing. But the Prosecution is entitled to respond, and the Trial Chamber would like to know whether the Prosecution intends to respond. And if this were the case, they would be entitled to three days to do so. Mr. Mundis, could you let us know what your position is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has nothing further to add. We will not be filing any further pleadings with respect to the certificate issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The Trial Chamber will address this matter a little later, and we will render an oral decision, as a decision will any case will be rendered in writing. Before giving the floor to the Defence team for its opening statement, I'd like to say that we have received from the Defence the overall witness list and schedule. Three witnesses should be called this week. One will testify for an hour and a half, the next witness will testify for six hours, and the third witness will testify for an hour and a half. Pursuant to our request, the Defence has indicated the list of documents which are likely to be tendered. This list identifies all those documents with exhibit numbers which have been reviewed on the 11th of October. Therefore, we have mapped out our schedule for the following week. I have asked the Defence team to provide us with a schedule over a two-week period. So we would like to have the schedule for the following week, please, the week after this one and the week after that, if it is at all possible. That said, I would now like to give the floor to the Defence, as the Defence is about to read its opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before I give the floor to my learned colleague, Mr. Bourgon, could I first of all inform you about something in relation to your decision, the one that you have just presented. Defence counsel has accepted your suggestion, and we will do our best to provide the witnesses scheduled and to provide you with the documents within a 15-day time limit. For the moment, this has not been possible because we were expecting to start with the expert witness for historical matters, but we have had to follow your decision and change the schedule. As a result, we weren't able to provide the complete list. And second, I would like to say that for the first witness in the list that we provided, we intended to examine this witness for an hour and a half. Could the Trial Chamber consider the possibility that this examination might take a little longer because we planned for this witness to arrive after a number of other witnesses who would already have informed the Trial Chamber of certain facts. But the Defence counsel would like to inform the Chamber that the examination will be finished this week, so we won't require additional time. As far as the opening statement is concerned, Mr. President, we have agreed that my colleague, Stephane Bourgon, should give the opening statement. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Edina Residovic. I shall now give the floor to your co-counsel, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet all members present in this courtroom. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I have the honour to address the Trial Chamber today with a view to reading the opening statement of the Defence. So pursuant to Article 82 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, to start off I do not hesitate, Your Honour, to tell you this is no mean task. To say the least, I must admit that I spent a long time thinking about what I should include in such an opening statement. If I were to plead before a jury today, this would not really raise any difficulties for me. If I were pleading before the martial court in Canada as I was accustomed to doing, I would know exactly what to say. But what kind of opening statement can I make in front of a Trial Chamber of an international tribunal? That is yet another question. This is why, Your Honour, after having discussed these matters with my colleague, I decided to opt for the following. I decided that the opening statement of the Defence will focus on the following objectives: In this opening statement, Your Honour, I'd like to inform you that it will last approximately three hours. I would like to identify what is at stake here for the accused. I would like to seize this opportunity to mention that you are able to follow my outline, the outline I intend following throughout the opening statement so you are able to keep up with what I am saying. As I was saying, the first thing I would like to address today in my opening -- in my opening statement will be to highlight the key issues. After that, I wish to take stock of current procedures to date and look into those -- the material evidence provided by the Prosecution which will be disputed during the Defence case. Of course, I shall also use the opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber of the evidence that will be presented and why we shall be presenting this evidence material. We should also, Your Honour, like to provide the Trial Chamber with a table which will enable all the people in the courtroom to understand the evidence material we are using. That said, Your Honour, I should like to draw your attention to the outline that is displayed on the screen. First of all, Your Honour, I shall start off with an introduction. The introduction will relate to what is at stake for the accused. This is broken down into nine parts. I shall first of all address the standard and the level of caution required on the part of a commander. I will then address the Prosecution case. We believe that this is indeed relevant at this stage of the procedure, so that the Trial Chamber is able to understand the evidence provided by the Defence. I shall then talk about factors pertaining to

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: who is the accused; what do we know about him; and what will we discover about this accused during the Defence case. We shall also address the Prosecution case and the Prosecution evidence presented by the Prosecution and also what was very specific. Also, as we have done since the beginning of the trial, we shall talk about the background and of its importance in this case. On the following page, Your Honour, you can see the various parts I shall address in my opening statement. We shall address the question of the witnesses which will be presented by the Defence counsel, the mujahedin factor. I shall make a few comments relating to the applicable law in this case, and I shall also discuss evidence material provided during the Defence case. I shall, of course, wrap this up with a conclusion, and I shall suggest an analysis grid to the Trial Chamber which can be used right until the end of the trial. Your Honour, I should now like to start on my introduction. The introduction will be divided into five parts. I think it is important, Your Honour, to understand what the duties and obligation of the Defence counsels are when presenting their case. I sahll talk about the strategy of the Defence counsels; and more specifically, as I have mentioned it, I shall say what the key issues are here and how important they are for the accused; I shall discuss what the purpose and objectives of the Defence team is when presenting its case; and lastly, Your Honour, the challenge we face in this particular stage of the trial. As far as the duty of the Defence counsels are concerned, as we start with the Defence case, Your Honour, we believe it is timely to take stock of our duties and obligations as Defence counsel. First of all, as the Trial Chamber already knows, all the Defence counsels are bound by the ethics committee that are here employed as attorneys before the International Tribunal. This lists our duties and obligations vis-a-vis our client, primarily, but vis-a-vis the Tribunal and the public at large. This is why, Your Honour, this quotation, we feel, is particularly relevant to this case and pertains specifically to the accused. It is important to explore each avenue without any fears whatsoever and without regarding any personal fears, with a view to highlighting those facts de jure and de facto, whilst not wasting too much time. This is what we have endeavoured to do since the beginning of this trial, and this is what we shall continue to do with all due respect to the International Tribunal. As far as the Defence strategy is concerned, we feel there's only one way of addressing this matter in this case. It is essential for us at a time we shall be presenting our case to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands the position of the accused and puts himself in the shoes of the accused. The Prosecution case which you have heard for some eight months is only one side of the story. We are now addressing the Defence case, and it is the opportunity for the accused to give his own story. We don't think that this is just an extension of the Prosecution case. Our objective in this particular stage of the -- of the trial and for the Trial Chamber at large is to unravel the truth. We certainly don't intend to confirm the Prosecution case; quite the contrary. For some eight months now, the Prosecution has adopted an approach which we feel is rather limited because the Prosecution did not ask the Trial Chamber to consider the background material overall. As you know, Your Honour, our approach is quite a different one. And if you like, the Prosecution has shown you the trees, but has not shown you the forest. These trees sometimes -- sometimes the trees had leaves and sometimes they did not because they were dead trees. So there's only one way we believe we can address this trial. We want to make sure, Your Honour, that you're able to put yourself in the accused's shoes. We have already had an opportunity to address the Rendulich case, and we believe that we should keep you abreast with the content of this case. General Rendulich was a German general. This general had to, over a hundred or so kilometres, had to backtrack and retreat because the Russian Army was coming towards the army and running behind his army corps. When exercising -- when complying with this order, General Rendulich pursued the policy of scorched earth, and he was accused of this in the proceedings known as "the high command trial." The conclusion reached by the Judges was the following one, Mr. President: Given the information that the Trial Chamber has at its disposal today, there is no doubt that the accused had no reason to pursue the policy of scorched earth. Nevertheless, at the time, given the circumstances prevailing and in view of what was possible for him to do and in view what he did do, the decision that he took was reasonable and he was acquitted on this count. The Rendulich principle, Mr. President, is a principle which has been adopted on a number of occasions, and in particular in the course of the negotiations at the diplomatic consequence which led to the adoption of the additional protocols to the Geneva Conventions. The Rendulich case is now better known in the military field and in the field of international humanitarian law. It is better known as the Rendulich amendment. A number of states, when they were ratifying the draft for the protocols additional to the Geneva Conventions, and in particular the first additional protocol, they insisted that a declaration of interpretation should be attached to this draft. They said that it was primordial, in their opinion, for commanders to be able to judged while taking into consideration the relevant circumstances at the time in question. Mr. President, I will pursue to address the matter or the key issues addressed by the Prosecution. This trial, Mr. President, is the trial of a commander. General Hadzihasanovic is before you because he was the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH Army. He is not here, Mr. President, because he himself personally committed crimes. He is here because the Prosecution claims that he failed to perform his duties as a commander. It is our position that the evidence has already demonstrated that this is not the case. And the evidence that the Defence counsel will present will lend additional support to this conclusion. Nevertheless, Mr. President, one should not forget -- and this is what we suggest when commencing with the Defence case: One should not forget that it is the exercise of command that is the object of this trial. The nature of the charges is, nevertheless, linked to crimes of war that were allegedly committed. The question is, Mr. President: Are the charges or the violations which General Hadzihasanovic allegedly failed to prevent, are the violations that he failed to prevent or punish such that they changed the way in which we should conduct this trial? We don't think that is the case, Mr. President. On the contrary. Not long ago, Mr. President, I had the opportunity of meeting a head of state, and I was asked to explain to this head of state what the position was of a member of Defence counsel. And to my great surprise, the reply that I could provide or that was provided was as follows: He must have done something to be there. This reply, Mr. President, astounded me. I cannot understand how today when we think about the legal rules, how can we believe that if an accused is before an international criminal tribunal, he must certainly have committed some crime. I believe, Mr. President, that it is of extreme importance to ensure that the rule of law and the presumption of innocence are principles which are maintained, principles to which one adheres by using all the means that this Tribunal has at its disposal. The purpose of this Tribunal, Mr. President, or one of its obvious objectives, is to do away with impugnity. As a starting point, this means that the highest norms must be respected, and one must base oneself on universal declarations. Crimes were committed in Central Bosnia in 1993. That appears to be the case. And this is definitely regrettable. The victims of these crimes merit all our compassion. But, Mr. President, this is not a reason to turn a commander into a scapegoat. What will the objective of the Defence be when presenting its evidence? First of all, Mr. President, we take note of the decision relating to the accused's motion for acquittal. This decision, Mr. President - and I believe that I can say this without showing disrespect - was a deceiving decision for us. Nevertheless, Mr. President, we respect the decision, and we will act accordingly. Mr. President, we will attempt to present a very good and coherent Defence case and won't leave anything to chance. We are prepared for this, and this is what we will do. Mr. President, our objective is as follows: We want to help the Trial Chamber to see beyond the poorly founded theory presented by the Prosecution. The challenge that we have is on your screen, Mr. President. Naturally, you have recognised this grand old dame, and perhaps you recognised in this figure a young maid. You have both figures on the screen. You have probably seen this image before. It is a drawing coming from the year 1915, and it is called "The Boring Figure." Mr. President, this is an image that contains two images, and it was developed to show us that the human brain can recognise only one of the figures contained in this figure at a given time. Mr. President, you may have identified a young woman or an old woman when looking at this image, but what the Defence counsel wants you to do is to look behind the smokescreen that the Prosecution has attempted to present you with. And now, Mr. President, I would like to address the first point of the opening statement: the level of caution and the standards that a commander should apply. I will first of all start addressing the issue of a theory, and then I will talk to you subsequently about the responsibility of a person in command position. According to the case law of the International Tribunal, there are three elements that have to be proved beyond any reasonable doubt if one is to deliver a verdict of guilty pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. These three elements relate to the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship; the second element has to do with the fact that the accused knew or had reason to know that violations were about to be committed or that violations had been committed. And thirdly, the accused failed to take reasonable measures in the circumstances. Mr. President, it seems to us, and this is evident for us, that there is an important difference between Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) of the Statute. In the case of 7(1), there's the proof of the actus reas, the material proof, and then there's the proof of intention, mens rea, that are used to arrive at a verdict of guilty. According to Article 7(3), Mr. President, this article doesn't have to do with the criminal intention. It has to do with imputed responsibility. In such a case, Mr. President, we require a norm, a referential norm that would enable the Chamber to evaluate in what manner the commander exercised his duties in 1993 in Central Bosnia. If we have a look at the third of the requisite elements, it is a question of necessary and reasonable measures that have to be taken. We believe that the word "necessary" and the word "reasonable" invoke a standard, invoke a certain level in light of which the acts committed by General Hadzihasanovic should be evaluated. With regard to the theory, the gap theory:, I believe, Mr. President, that it is important to understand that the Defence representing General Hadzihasanovic does not intend to minimise the importance of a role of a commander. A little over ten years ago, I was involved in proceedings in Canada, the proceedings against a commander of an air regiment in Canada, an airborne regiment, and this regiment allegedly committed certain violations, certain offences when in operation in Somalia. This was a disgrace for Canada. This trial was a disgrace for Canada, and the government even dismissed this regiment from the Canadian Forces. The commander of this regiment was accused in front of the court-martial. As part of the Defence, I was a junior lawyer involved in the case, and this person was acquitted of the charges against him; namely, of the charge of having given orders that were contrary to the rules of engagement he had been provided with by the government. In spite of the acquittal, Mr. President, the person in question, Lieutenant Colonel Mathieu, had his life ruined. In spite of the fact he was acquitted, his life was ruined. And from that date onwards, I understood the importance of the role of a commander in the army. Although I had already been a member of the army for ten years at the time, and today before you, it is in no way my intention to minimise the role of a commander. On the contrary, my intention today, Mr. President, is to present evidence for the Defence which will demonstrate to the Trial Chamber that General Hadzihasanovic did everything he could and performed his duties in the circumstances that prevailed in Central Bosnia in 1993. In order to do this, Mr. President, I think it is important to ask oneself the following question: What was the objective of rendering commanders responsible? Why are we here today? Why are we with an accused who himself did not commit any crimes? And why do we, and I'm referring to the international community, represented by the Prosecution, why have we decided to level charges against a commander? First of all, Mr. President, the reason is that the objective of rendering commanders' responsibility is to respect international humanitarian law. The objective is to prevent infractions of international humanitarian law. The objective of commander's responsibility is to ensure commanders of the military who are involved in operations are placed under responsible command and that they are held accountable for the acts of their insubordinates [as interpreted]. Mr. President, we have to ask ourselves how we are going to proceed to evaluate the work of a commander on this standard. How can one find out whether General Hadzihasanovic in the circumstances that prevailed at the time did everything that he could and performed all his duties? There is one possible reference that we can invoke, Mr. President, and this is the trial of the General Yamashita. We have already addressed this issue in our pre-trial brief. On the 25th of September 1945, General Yamashita was accused as follows: Between the 9th of October 1944 and the 2nd of September 1945, and that's a period of approximately 11 months, at Manila and other place in the Philippine Islands, while in command of the armed forces of Japan at war with the the United States of America, unlawfully disregarded and failed to discharge his duty as commander to control the operations of the members of his command, permitting them to commit brutal atrocities and other grave crimes against the people of the United States and of its allies, and in particular, against the people of the Philippines. And for this reason, he was accused of having committed violations and having failed to respect the laws of war. Mr. President, this is a very serious charge. Nevertheless, the reason for which I wanted to refer to this case is that in the case of General Yamashita, there was one charge, and a series of crimes were listed as having been committed by subordinates. General Yamashita had only been charged with one count, and he had been charged with having failed to perform his duties. This is the danger we are facing in this case, Mr. President, since rather than having to confront only one charge, General Hadzihasanovic has to confront a number of specific charges. And the Prosecution has tried to make separate or list separate charges against the accused. Mr. President, when dealing with the responsibility of the General and when attempting to evaluate evidence for the Defence, we believe that the question one should first ask is whether General Hadzihasanovic performed his role or not. We should ask ourselves whether he did everything that was his duty, given the circumstances that prevailed in 1993. Mr. President, the responsibilities of a commander pursuant to 7(3) of the Statute shouldn't be strictly defined. There is a difference, Mr. President. Strict responsibility is such that the accused would be declared to be guilty for the simple fact that he was the commander of the subordinate who committed a crime. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, we are fortunately protected against such a strict definition of responsibility. And this is a principle that we have invoked on a number of occasions and that we will invoke on a number of occasions in the course of the Defence counsel. But Mr. President, how should one differentiate between the commander -- or a commander who is responsible and reasonable from a commander who failed to perform his duties? Mr. President, at what point in time does the conduct of a commander become criminal? At what point in time could such a commander be held criminally liable? We believe, Mr. President, that this quote that I have referred to is one that could help us in this case. Mr. President, this is a quote taken from the Yamashita case, and where one says "Where the commander deviates significantly from customary command practices and war crimes are committed by subordinates as a direct result, the commander may be guilty of underlying offences just as if he had committed them himself." The second quote, Mr. President, comes from the High Command case, and according to this quote, "there must be a personal dereliction" - I'm looking for the right word in French to translate the terms "personal dereliction" in English - "there must be a failure to supervise his subordinates that constitutes criminal negligence on his part." And the manner of determining whether there is criminal negligence means that there must be "personal neglect amounting to a wanton, immoral disregard of the action of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence." This is a lack of care, an extreme case of insouciance. It involves not taking into consideration what subordinates do or might do, and as a result, this shows in a way that a commander agrees or supports the violations committed by his subordinates. Mr. President, we believe that when discussing the required level of caution, when we're talking about standards, when we're talking about how the Trial Chamber will evaluate whether the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic are such that he should be declared guilty of crimes, we believe that this is a standard that the Trial Chamber should refer to when evaluating these matters. Naturally, Mr. President, we do not believe that General Hadzihasanovic, by his acts and by the manner in which he exercised his command - and this is what you will hear from witnesses and what you will see in documents, and you will have already seen this in some documents that have been presented in the case - we believe that General Hadzihasanovic doesn't even approach this standard, the standard that relates to the responsibility of a commander. Mr. President, it's also important to remind oneself that the responsibility of a commander is not an obligation that ensues from the results, that is based on results. What do we mean when we say this? It's simple, Mr. President. When a commander discovers that a crime is just about to be committed or when a commander discovers that a crime is being committed by subordinates, if the commander takes necessary and reasonable measures to prevent this crime from being committed, it is not important whether the crime has been committed or not, in such a case, the commander should be acquitted. As far as punishment is concerned, if a commander discovers that a violation was committed, that a crime was committed and if the commander takes the necessary and reasonable measures in the light of the circumstances prevailing, whether the alleged perpetrator is punished or not at the end doesn't change the fact that the commander performed his duties and should not be declared guilty of this crime. This is similar what we discover in the Krnojelac case, Trial Chamber II, where it is stated that the commander does not have to perform the impossible. A commander has the duty to exercise his powers within the limits of those same powers. This quotation, Your Honour, was quoted by the Appeals Chamber, by the Prosecution in its brief, and by the Defence team also in its brief. A commander cannot perform the impossible. The level of caution is a requirement. Your Honour, I should now like to address the second part of my opening statement, i.e., the Prosecution case. We believe, as I have stated a little earlier on, that this is a prerequisite in order to get a good understanding of what lies at stake in this trial, before addressing the Defence case. Your Honour, I'd like to submit to you that the Prosecution case can be broken down into five parts: The objective of the Prosecution; the initial Prosecution case; the reversal of the Prosecution case; the new Prosecution case presented by the Prosecution; and lastly, the limited approach of the Prosecution. I shall start off with the objective or the aim of the Prosecution. This quotation is a quotation taken directly from the Prosecution case. I think it is important, Your Honour, to read this through. This is what the Prosecution lawyers have presented to this Trial Chamber on 2nd of December last. This is the other side of the same coin relating to a number of trials already being heard before this International Tribunal. The most important cases were that of the Prosecution versus Blaskic and the Prosecution versus Kordic and Cerkez as such. "In this trial against Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura, stated that all the parties to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, even though this was deployed in different regions and on different scales, have violated the international humanitarian law which comes under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. This trial and the material evidence we will present will demonstrate that the war crimes that were committed -- that war crimes were committed by both parties to the conflict in Central Bosnia and the trial will clearly indicate to the rest of the world, give a broader picture and in-depth picture of the war in Bosnia." Your Honour, as far as the first point is concerned, namely, the other side of the coin, what is the other side of the same coin and what was the Prosecution referring to? The facts, namely in the Blaskic and Kordic cases, to only quote these two, for which the Prosecution wish to demonstrate the other side of the same coin. Your Honour, if you will bear with me for a few minutes, I have a technical problem to solve. Your Honour, I think I didn't press on the right button. If you will allow me just a few extra minutes, please. Your Honour, this is a quote from the opening statement of the Prosecution in the trial the Prosecutor versus Blaskic. Once again, Your Honour, I think it is important to read this quote which is dated the 24th of June 1997. This is now being read in English. [In English] "The case over which you... will preside is case about how Bosnian Croat military forces under the command and control of Tihomir Blaskic ethnically cleansed partss of Central Bosnia in 1993 by systematically attacking Muslim civilians and their homes and destroying their property and by employing methods that no responsible military commander would condone. The illegal methods used by his forces were calculated to achieve an ethnic majority for the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia." [Interpretation] Without making any further comments vis-a-vis these accusations, so other trials against Bosnian Croats, I think one can by just looking at this quotation understand why the Prosecution wishes to show the other side of the same coin. The International Tribunal is criticised for its lack of impartiality. The Defence has every interest, therefore, in showing the other side. But I would like to make two provisos. There are two pitfalls we would like to avoid: (A), the danger of rewriting history; but even worse than that, the danger of pinpointing a scapegoat on the other side. The Prosecution did not state at the beginning of this trial "This is a trial of a commander who did not meet his obligations. This is the trial of a commander who should be punished to -- so that the rest of the world understands what complying with international humanitarian law means and what happened in Central Bosnia." What the Prosecution stated was that this was a trial to show the other side of the coin. We think this is a very important question when addressing the strategy of the Prosecution and the Prosecution case. The second point, Your Honour, I would like to address relates to the issue of the mujahedin. During the cross-examination, an investigator clearly identified the mujahedin factor and stated this was an essential component in this case. I shall quote in English: [In English] "Question: So the crimes committed by the mujahedin was an important aspect of your investigation?" [Interpretation] The answer was: Yes, it was." [In English] Question: And as part of the investigation proposal that was approved, finding out persons responsible for the crimes committed by the mujahedin was one of your principle objectives. I can rephrase that if you want. I'm just suggesting to you that you made an investigation proposal. Is that correct?" "Yes, members of the team did." "And in that investigation proposal, you have targets, or issues? What is the term do you use?" "We would use -- targets is appropriate." "Target it will be. And one of those targets were crimes committed by the mujahedin?" "That's correct." [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have heard as evidence mujahedin committed crimes in Central Bosnia in 1993. But the evidence we will present will clearly indicate that the tragic events that took place in Miletici, in Maline, in Orasac, to only name a few - were committed by mujahedin. Once again, Your Honour, it is easy to understand the objective of the Prosecution, i.e., to find a guilty person for the crimes -- for these crimes. We support them in this endeavour, but we cannot support them when they tend to turn Enver Hadzihasanovic into a scapegoat. The evidence heard to date and the evidence to be heard in the future confirms that this is not the case. How does the Prosecution case stand to date? I should rather say, the method used by the Prosecution to demonstrate the guilt of the accused. Thereby, we are able to assess two things: First of all, the knowledge Hadzihasanovic had of those crimes. The Prosecution used three important -- raised three important issues which we shall also address. The question of notice or having had the information that crimes were about to be committed or had been committed. The question of notice, Your Honour, was addressed once again by the Appeals Chamber as it rendered its decision in the Blaskic case. The question of having been informed or not is not something which rests on a suggestion or a presumption. It does not rest on the fact that the accused should have known; it's a question which rests on the following: The accused must have had the information enabling him to infer that a violation was about to be committed or had been committed. Once again, as far as the question of knowledge is concerned, the Prosecution has used, in its opening statement and in its pre-trial brief, has mentioned the question of orders stating that an accused -- when an accused or the accused gave orders to his men not to steal, this means that the same commander knew that his men were looting and destroying property. Once again, this question was addressed in the recent decision in the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case where it was stated that if a commander gives an order with a view to preventing his subordinates from committing any form of violation, such an order cannot be deemed or compared with the knowledge he might have thereof. The question -- next question is how the crimes are related to one another. On reading the Prosecution pre-trial brief, it is important to understand that the knowledge of the accused pertains to -- from one crime to another as the accused has the information on Dusina, he is also held responsible for Miletici. As he had the knowledge regarding Miletici, he is therefore responsible for Miletici [as interpreted]. We believe that this is an argument which goes round in circles. And this cannot be used to demonstrate that the accused had the required knowledge. Also, the -- in the Prosecution case, we have outlined the key issue, in other words, the fact that the accused did not take the necessary measures despite the resources he had at his disposal. Once again, a quotation from the opening statement of the Prosecution dated 2nd of December: The accused was -- the Prosecution was going to prove something which related to the heart of the matter, that the accused had not taken the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent these criminal offences from being committed or from punishing the perpetrators thereof. The only issue we can agree on with the Prosecution is that we are here dealing with something which has to do with the heart of the matter. The General Hadzihasanovic, did he or did he not take the necessary and reasonable measures, given the circumstances? In this case, Your Honour, we believe that the General Hadzihasanovic has taken all the necessary measures given the circumstances. What was the Prosecution case when the question of measures was raised? Once again, I quote from the opening statement of the Prosecution. We get an insight into what the Prosecution deems are the right measures a commander should take; namely, this is stipulated in the Geneva Conventions. They instruct the subordinates and the soldiers of their duties and obligation in line to international law, to order and subordinate and comply with international humanitarian law, and all violations of the latter should be punished. The fact that disciplinary measures should be imposed with a view to complying with the rules and regulations of the Bosnian Army, and make sure that all the necessary measures to implement and comply with these measures are actually taken. In the following page is dealt all the measures that the Prosecution felt a reasonable commander should take. Your Honour, we don't feel that this quotation, even though we have mentioned it in our opening statement, we don't think that this has been supported by any testimony or any document adduced by the Prosecution. We would therefore like to ask the Trial Chamber which measures should be taken, either based on the law or on interpretation of a number of documents which have been adduced by the Prosecution or by the witnesses that were called in. The Defence case or the Defence intends to fill this gap and intends to explain which measures a reasonable commander should take and why. The Prosecution case, Your Honour, can be summed up as follows: There were three letters sent to the Public Prosecutor, to Travnik, to the court of Travnik, and the cantonal court of Zenica. These three documents clearly demonstrate what the Prosecution case is all about. For the Prosecution, the only important measure when it conducted its investigation in this case, when it prepared this case, the only measure was as follows: It was important to understand whether the accused had taken the necessary measures or whether a -- any soldier in the 3rd Corps had been tried for a war crime. The expert witness presented by the Prosecution demonstrated that the measures taken by a commander can be of different nature. And if a person is tried for a war crime, there can be a number of reasons for this. Nevertheless, in one of these documents, the president of the cantonal court of Travnik, Exhibit P773, the president of the cantonal court of Travnik confirmed that 857 cases had been dealt with by the military district court. But the Prosecution did not look into the matter, for it was after war crimes. I shall now talk about the reversal of the Prosecution case. This could be explained in several ways: (a), the measures taken by the accused; and (b), the conclusion of the expert witness of the Prosecution as he answered one of the questions put to him by the Trial Chamber. We know that the Prosecution case could no longer hold true after the expert witness stated "I have seen a number of additional documents that prove that General Hadzihasanovic not only gave orders, not only complied with the various stages of the procedure to check that everybody was being treated legally, looking into the perpetrators mentioned in this document. But I changed my mind when I say that he had not followed up on all of this after having taken a decision, and quite obviously he did." The documents adduced, Your Honour, even though these only represent a sample of all the measures undertaken by the accused, go well and way beyond those measures put forward by the Prosecution. The conclusion of the Prosecution representative ran as follows, and I am quoting him here: "After having filed these documents, you may remember that when these documents were presented for the first time, the Prosecution did not know that these documents existed. It seemed quite clear and contrary to our initial viewpoint, the accused had done nothing other than what General Reinhardt had been able to identify. One case, it seemed that the accused had taken the necessary and reasonable measures, and we find ourselves now in a different situation. It seems pretty well clear that on several occasions, the security department of the 3rd Corps did conduct investigations and transferred all these cases to the military district courts so that the necessary measures be taken. Thereby, he met his obligation. It is important to understand that once an commander has conducted an investigation and that he has transferred the investigation and sent it to the competent tribunal, that's where his obligation ends." This was a conclusion put forward by the Prosecution, and this is a new conclusion. I should like to quote what was stated on the 4th of June 2004 which I would entitle "the new Prosecution case." And I am quoting from what was said on that day in English. [In English] "Mr. President, Your Honours, the investigation team leader is currently in Bosnia with an investigation team, again through court records and district military prosecutor's records in order to hopefully satisfy the Chamber that steps were not taken by units of the 3rd Corps to punish the perpetrators of the crimes that are set forth in the indictment. So the point is not for the investigator to return with a large number of documents, but precisely the opposite. The team that is currently searching through, again, the court archives is attempting to demonstrate that there are no such records pertaining to the crimes that are set forth in the Third Amended Indictment. The subject matter of that proposed testimony would be to the effect that teams of investigators have again gone through the court records, and there are no records indicating that the crimes in the Third Amended Indictment were the subject of referrals by the 3rd Corps or its subordinate units. So it's not a question of coming back with additional documents; it's a question of testifying as to the lack thereof." [Interpretation] Mr. President, having taken note of the reverse of the theory -- or the Prosecution having confirmed the reversal of their theory, the Defence believed naively that this could put an end to the trial because the evidence showed that the accused, General Hadzihasanovic, had acted as a responsible commander. And we would like to remind you, Mr. President, that that is the purpose of this trial. Nevertheless, the Prosecution, when establishing its new theory, wanted to show that measures hadn't been taken for the specific crimes contained in the indictment. And secondly, they wanted to show that they would prove this by sending a team to Central Bosnia. We know what happened afterwards, Mr. President. The Chamber was able to determine that the mission, in extremis of the Prosecution conducted in Central Bosnia, was not such that one could claim beyond any reasonable doubt that measures were not taken with regard to all the counts in the indictment. I'll come back to this later. Nevertheless, what is even more important is that the Prosecution did not explain, nor did it attempt to explain, why a commander who took over 1.000 steps, 1.000 measures against his soldiers, measures for violations similar to those mentioned in the indictment, why according to the Prosecution he would -- why would such a commander fail to take measures in certain specific cases. Mr. President, this theory quite simply does not tally with the evidence in the case. I have one other matter I'd like to address, and then perhaps we could have a break. We could then finish with the restrictive nature of the evidence. Since the beginning of the case, Mr. President, we believe that the Prosecution is trying to limit the proceedings to certain, very specific items. The Prosecution is not trying to reduce the length of the trial. That is our submission. They could have limited the evidence concerning the crime base or concerning specific crimes, and they could have presented more elements concerning the conduct of General Hadzihasanovic. However, this is not how they proceeded, and the reason for this, Mr. President, is as follows: We believe that the Prosecution is trying to ensure that the Chamber does not examine the exercise of command on the part of General Hadzihasanovic in the light of the overall context, in the light of the armed conflict reigning in Central Bosnia in 1993. For reasons that I have already mentioned, in the course of the Defence case, we will strive to demonstrate the necessity of taking into account the overall context so as to be able to evaluate in what manner General Hadzihasanovic exercised his command. Mr. President, I note that it is half past 3.00, and I suggest that we have a break now, and after the break I will address the third issue.
