utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume. Mr. Bourgon, you may take the floor to continue with your opening statement. 2

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May it please the Court. Mr. President, Your Honours, I will now move on to the third part of the Defence's opening statement, which has to do with factors pertaining to the accused. And under this heading, Mr. President, and as illustrated on the screen, I would like to show that what Prosecution witnesses said with regard to General Hadzihasanovic, and I would like to also mention what Defence witnesses will say with regard to the accused. I will address what the Prosecution witnesses have said and what Defence witnesses will say. First of all, we know that there are witnesses, there's the Witness Garrod, the Witness Duncan, and the Witness Watters. And I intend to use them as examples. I will start with Witness Duncan who said the following, Mr. President: The question was as follows: "You met him on 18 or 20 occasions. You were in that zone for six months, General, at the time. What impression did you obtain with regard to the competence, the aptitude, and the military capacities of General Hadzihasanovic, and in particular in relation to the exercise of command over his troops in the 3rd Corps zone, in the zone of the BH Army 3rd Corps?" And General Duncan's response was that "as an officer, I thought that General Hadzihasanovic was extremely intelligent. He was an exceptionally capable and competent commander." Further on in the course of the cross-examination, General Duncan added that this was a good description of Hadzihasanovic. He was a very competent and capable man. And my second quote comes from Sir Martin Garrod. The Defence put a question to this witness, and at the very end of the cross-examination, it was said: "I tried to see how -- I am trying to see how you met this man, General Hadzihasanovic, in the field in 1993. I spoke to you about the measures taken in relation to disciplinary matters and in relation to instructions, communications, information from his superiors, information from international representatives with whom he had contact. When taking all this into consideration, I would like to ask you about your opinion of the personality and the character of General Hadzihasanovic. And given everything we have discussed today and given the knowledge that you have and given your meetings with this man in 1993, would you say that this is a commander who would not take any measures to punish someone if it is possible to take such measures?" And the answer was: "What is certain is that in my opinion, he was a good general which necessarily implies everything which you have just stated." And finally, Mr. President, a quote from the Witness Bryan Watters, an international witness, a deputy command of BritBat. He said that Hadzihasanovic was an exceptional military commander in all aspects, at least -- and in particular in comparison to his counterpart in the HVO, Blaskic. Mr. President, I could provide you with a number of similar quotes or identical quotes, but there's also something that has already been stated by the Prosecution. And this is something that we will prove in relation to General Hadzihasanovic. We will return to the fact that this is a career officer, an officer who was given a position that was higher than the one he had at the beginning of the armed conflict. This was an officer who was placed in a situation which was quite impossible. He was an officer who worked 20 hours a day, 7 days a week. And he almost died of exhaustion towards the end of the summer of 1993. This is what witnesses will say in front of this Chamber. But in spite of everything, this is a man who always seemed to be in full control of himself. This is the very same man who took numerous measures to improve command and control within the 3rd Corps, this very same commander who never hesitated to take measures to prevent and to put an end to the conflict with the HVO. Mr. President, witnesses will appear before this Trial Chamber to testify that General Hadzihasanovic pushed them to the limits of what can be tolerated and to the limits of what can be accepted on the part of an officer, and they were requested not to take up arms, not to attack, not to mix with the HVO. This very same commander took multiple measures to train his personnel, to train his staff. I have to slow down, Mr. President, for the sake of the interpretation. This is an officer who, as I have just said, never hesitated to take measures to prevent and to put an end to the conflict with the HVO. This very same commander took steps to form and to train the 3rd Corps members. This commander on numerous occasions demanded of his subordinate commanders that they take measures against all violations of international humanitarian law. This commander incessantly asked his subordinate commanders to report to him, and he put into place a system to facilitate the exchange of information within the 3rd Corps. This very same commander never hesitated to recommend to his superior headquarters that they should try to improve the 3rd Corps. And as an example, Mr. President, I mention the creation of operational groups. And this goes together with the Prosecution's expert witness who was asked about what one calls "the span of control." Another example that I could provide you with, Mr. President, is that there were recommendations from the 3rd Corps division to a different course. And as another example, I could mention the report prepared by General Hadzihasanovic with regard to the shortcomings of the military judicial system by the district court, or in the case of the district courts in Zenica and Travnik. This same commander, Mr. President, used his military police battalion to an extreme. This was in order to ensure that there was discipline within the 3rd Corps. Mr. President, witnesses will appear before this Chamber to say that if there is only one accused who is now being held in the UN Detention Unit who, on the basis of his conduct merits the title of general, that general would be General Hadzihasanovic. There are witnesses who will be appearing before this Chamber to say that General Hadzihasanovic would not accept any secondary measures, any measures of a lower order. They will come to testify before this Chamber that if it was possible for him to take any measures, he would never have hesitated to do so. Mr. President, all of this demonstrates and will demonstrate that the theory presented by the Prosecution doesn't hold water. Why would a commander of such a kind, why would the commander who has all these qualities, a commander who had taken all these measures, why would he have omitted or why would he have failed to take measures in certain specific instances? I will now move on to the fourth part of my opening statement which has to do with the evidence presented by the Prosecution, evidence that will be contested. And Mr. President, I can see that there's a special mistake on the screen before you, and I apologise for that. These are the concerns of the witnesses for the Prosecution, Mr. President. One should note that the Prosecution didn't find the means of introducing witnesses from the 3rd Corps. Nevertheless, Mr. President, a number of Defence witnesses will be witnesses from the 3rd Corps. We believe that this is a factor that should be taken into consideration. Mr. President, the issue of -- as far as the issue of international witnesses is concerned, in one of its submissions, the Prosecution claimed that international witnesses were useful, they were impartial, and they can provide very -- that they can provide the Trial Chamber with very precious information. But as my colleague stated -- my colleague who represents the second accused in this case -- this depends whether the same international witnesses were direct witnesses of the events or whether they are just conveying hearsay information. Mr. President, we believe that the Trial Chamber is in a position to differentiate between an international witness who relayed relevant information on the basis of the duties he had performed from another witness who relayed information which was second-hand information or even third-hand information. We believe that the Chamber can make this distinction. We will be presenting international -- we will be calling international witnesses, Mr. President, witnesses from the 3rd Corps as well, and all these witnesses are prepared to come and testify. The question of the expert witness, Mr. President, we have heard General Reinhardt, one of the Prosecution's expert witnesses. He is a respected man, and he was the deputy commander of NATO during a given period of time. And this is no small matter. Nevertheless, Mr. President, the Prosecution approached this witness as he wasn't only an expert in matters of command and in military matters. The Prosecution tried to present this witness as one who was an expert in legal matters, as an expert who had good knowledge of the way in which the BH Army functioned, as a witness who was an expert as far as mujahedin issues are concerned, and an expert in international law. Naturally, at the end of the trial, we will have the opportunity of demonstrating the extent to which this testimony is flawed. But for the moment, we are preparing to present our evidence, and we will be calling expert witnesses, Mr. President. I will be in a position to tell you who they are and what they will be testifying about in the near future. And then there's the matter of the Prosecution's documentary evidence, which consists of about 1.000 documents. How many of these documents were identified by witnesses? Very few of them. The documents were admitted; they were tendered into evidence as if they had certain relevance and as if they contained a sufficient level of reliability. Mr. President, we believe that these documents, even though there are witnesses who drafted them and testified about them, we believe that this is an important factor which should be taken into consideration when the Defence presents its evidence. Mr. President, there are certain flaws in the Prosecution's evidence, and we would like to draw your attention to these flaws. We believe, Mr. President, that these flaws could swing this case in one particular direction. We haven't heard about the historical context, very little, only a limited number of statements in the Prosecution's opening statement. In the course of the Prosecution's case, we heard nothing about the political context. And in particular, we heard nothing about the Vance-Owen Plan which in our opinion - and we will have the opportunity to discuss this subject - is a key element in relation to what happened in Central Bosnia in 1993. We heard very little about the constitutional context, and naturally, it's by no means advantageous of the Prosecution to say that the BH government was in favour of a multi-ethnic country. It would be advantageous for the Prosecution to say that the responsibilities of the accused -- or to proceed in a manner that would clearly identify the accused's responsibilities before this Trial Chamber. We believe, nevertheless, Mr. President, that this was the Prosecution's responsibility to explain all these matters, at least to limit the debate. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But even worse, Mr. President, is the fact that the Prosecution keeps using the term "zone of control" or "area of responsibility." This is an issue that was raised long before the beginning of this trial. We believe that the matter has been settled by the Pre-Trial Judge. Nevertheless, in the Prosecution's submissions, they continue to use the terms "zone of control" and "area of responsibility" in order to try to make this an element of importance in relation to the superior-subordinate relationship. We have heard very little, Mr. President, about the opposition to the difficult context or difficult situation that General Hadzihasanovic found himself in. The Prosecution kept trying to close the debate. We will do the contrary, Mr. President. We will open the debate, and we will provide such evidence to the Trial Chamber. As far as the context within command was exercised, Mr. President, and we have mentioned this on a number of occasions already, the purpose of this trial is to deal with the responsibility of the commander. But the Prosecution in its evidence did not present any information, any details about the number of units under General Hadzihasanovic. There was no organisation chart representing the 3rd Corps. There was no organisation chart representing the command structure of the 3rd Corps. No information was presented on the way in which the 3rd Corps functioned, apart from in the case of witnesses who came at the very beginning of the trial, witnesses who were supposed to testify for the Defence. There was very little information about the problems encountered by General Hadzihasanovic. The Prosecution has tried to minimise the effect, the impact of these problems. In a response to a request from the Defence to have certain facts admitted - the 23rd of March was the date - there was opposition to certain adjudicated facts on the exercise of command. And we will have the opportunity to return to this issue. I will now move on to the factual context. The flaws in relation to the factual context have already been discussed. But I would like to make a few general observations. As far as the identity of the alleged perpetrators of crime are concerned, this has been to be date 12/1:53. There's the question of the identity of the units involved. There's very little information about these subjects that would allow the Trial Chamber to establish superior-subordinate relationship. To the extent that this is possible, we will provide the relevant information concerning the location of 3rd Corps units at critical moments. Mr. President, as far as the question of destruction is concerned, and this is a relevant example, we have nothing about the destruction that occurred in 1993. We have nothing about the precise dates. The indictment doesn't refer to any precise dates. There is mention of facts, or information collected by witnesses who had second-, third-, or fourth-hand information. Yet, there were investigators who were available. And finally as far as the issue of the presence of the mujahedin is concerned, there were rumours, there were comments, there were observations, videos which appeared out of the blue, and the Prosecution attempted to narrate a story that did not tally with actual events on the ground. Mr. President, these flaws are flaws that the Defence will try to correct. And Defence counsel will attempt to provide the necessary information to the Trial Chamber to the extent that this is possible. But what is even more important is the question of the measures taken by the accused during the period relevant to the indictment. We have had opportunity to address the matter of measures taken by the accused. But what is even more important is that we are involved in proceedings that deal with the command responsibility. And as the Prosecution stated, the issue of the measures taken goes to the heart of the matter. Nevertheless, nothing was said and nothing was done with regard to the military court of the 3rd Corps. This was a court that existed within the heart of the 3rd Corps command. Nothing was said, no investigations were conducted with regard to the existence of special military courts. When we discussed the issue of subordinate units, Mr. President, on the basis of documents that have been tendered, there is evidence that certain criminal plans were presented not only by the command of the 3rd Corps but also by subordinate units of General Hadzihasanovic. These matters were not investigated. As far as the military police battalion is concerned, and I alluded to this issue a little earlier on, the Prosecution in its opening statement said that the accused even had a military police battalion. Subordinate units had military police battalions, but they did not do anything. Or as I'm referring to Exhibit DH155/3 which is in evidence, it says that monthly reports for the 3rd Corps military police battalion, it says that there were 22.700 persons who were checked at checkpoints. There were 256 individuals detained for a period of under 24 hours. 25 individuals were detained for a 24-hour period in accordance with the law. 1.500 vehicles were checked to see whether they contained goods that had been stolen. 24 criminal reports had been filed against 32 individuals, 3 were for war crimes; 1 for an act of genocide; 1 for arm rebellion; 1 for a serious offence; 1 for homicide; 1 for murder; 4 for theft; 6 for a special form of theft; 1 for espionage; and 1 for failing to perform one's obligatory military service. These were the results of the of the military police batallion of the 3rd Corps, and this covers a one-month period. In the course of the presentation of its evidence, Defence counsel will demonstrate that such evidence quite simply does not fit in with the theory presented by the Prosecution, according to which in certain cases the accused failed to take measures. Your Honour, I should like to address the fifth point, i.e., how important background material is. I mentioned earlier on the flaws in the Prosecution case that did not address the issue of background material. I also stated that we would establish a distinction here and clearly talk about background material. I've already talked about the Rendulic case, and I shall not go over it again. The question of the difference between the charges pursuant to Articles 7(1) and 7(1) [as interpreted] justify my addressing it here. "If an accused or commander of a unit" -- 7(1) and 7(3) -- "has personally committed a crime, if the same commander has taken part personally in a crime, the context is not so important. But in this particular case, when the commander has never committed any crime, that this commander has taken a number of measures to prevent and punish the perpetrators of the crimes, the context then becomes crucial. This context is not something we are going to be using in our arguments. This context is addressed today to enable the Trial Chamber to understand what the work of General Hadzihasanovic entailed in the light of the situation he was facing at the time. The Defence will, therefore, in this particular -- at this particular stage of the proceedings will address the historical, political, and military background in this case. As far as the historical background is concerned, the Trial Chamber has already informed us of the fact that it was interested in having a historical view of the situation pertaining to the 1990s. We felt it was important to go back even further in time. You may have already read the report of our historical expert. It is important, in our opinion, that this witness come to the Trial Chamber and say to the Judges that the territory of Bosnia was always recognised, with the exception of a short interval during the Second World War. It is important for our Defence, Your Honour, to hear the expert witness that as regards a history of Bosnia, there always has been a multi-ethnic community and multicultural community living in this country. People from different ethnic backgrounds lived together and lived alongside each other. The historical expert will tell you, just to give you an example, will tell you where the differences lie, by quoting Switzerland, for instance, by quoting Switzerland. The citizens enjoy a different status, but it is easy to understand that they are spread in different regions or areas of Switzerland. The same applies to Belgium where people live in different areas, and you can locate each group according to geographical areas. But this was not the case in Bosnia because people of different ethnic backgrounds shared the same areas. The four main religions were living alongside each other in Bosnia, whereas in other countries in Europe, religion tended to overrule a number of other things. So it's very important that the historical expert come and talk to the Trial Chamber about these matters, that the expert witness tell the Trial Chamber that the Commission Badinter was looking into this, was trying to understand whether the regions of the former Yugoslavia did have the prerequisite conditions to become independent states once again. Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1992, on the 6th of April, did fulfil all the prerequisite opinions set out by the Commission Badinter in a democratic way and was recognised as an independent country. On that same day, Bosnia-Herzegovina was attacked. In the middle of 1992, Your Honour, nearly half the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was already occupied by the Serb forces. Bosnia-Herzegovina was not prepared for war. This has been mentioned, by the way, on several occasions by the Prosecution in the Blaskic case. The defence mechanisms for citizens, the famous All People's Defence system, the system which had been used before and the independence of Bosnia was, therefore, prevented from happening. The political platform adopted by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be explained to you by this expert witness. And in line with the historical situation of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be addressed. Bosnia-Herzegovina wished to have a multi-ethnic country, notwithstanding different religious faiths and a number of other criteria, and more importantly, which is what the expert witness will tell us, was not able to achieve what it was after. It was impossible to divide Bosnia without resorting to ethnic cleaning, and this was against the ambitions of its government. The political background, Your Honour, is my next point. On the 22nd of May, Bosnia-Herzegovina became a member of the United Nations and became a fully fledged member of the United Nations. And as such, Bosnia-Herzegovina was entitled to be protected by the other member states of the United Nations. Rather than protecting Bosnia-Herzegovina, the country was under an embargo. And because of this embargo, the country was unable to find the weapons it needed to protect its country, whereas on the Serb side, the Federal Socialist Republic of Serbia supported this. And on the Croatian side, they were supported by Croatia. And more importantly, an expert witness will come and tell you that whilst Central Bosnia was striving to become an independent state, the Croats in Bosnia were setting up a political party and a parallel government which turned into, then, a parallel armed force. The Vance-Owen Plan, which I mentioned earlier on, Your Honour, was probably what led to the separation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on an ethnic basis. This was a foundation of the plan. We have already had the opportunity to hear an expert discuss this, discuss the acts of the Croats in Bosnia with a view to implementing the Vance-Owen Plan by force, before the Vance-Owen Plan had even been adopted. Lastly, Your Honour, the anti-Bosnian propaganda by the HVO forced transfer of people under the pretense of an attack in Bosnia-Herzegovina; the objectives of the HVO, which were destroy the civil bodies, set up parallel organisations, and to set up and conquer an independent territory. Just as this very simple issue of propaganda we have heard a lot about already; nevertheless, we would like to file a number of documents in this regard, and we believe our historical expert witness will be able to explain these documents. There was a political will on the part of the HVO. As soon as it came to discussing the Bosnian Army, it was addressed as "Muslim forces" or "MOS" or "mujahedin." This was a propaganda tool which was used by the HVO. The constitutional background, Your Honour, i.e., the running of the state, the system in which command responsibility and position of the commander was established. Most of the documents used by the constitutional expert witness have already been filed before this Trial Chamber, but there are a greater number of documents still to be filed. The constitutional expert will explain which laws applied at the time; which laws were replaced, i.e., the former laws; and which laws remained unchanged at the time Bosnia-Herzegovina became a sovereign and independent state. We need to understand the limited responsibility and position of the accused. We feel this is a crucial issue, the type of conflict we're dealing with. We have discussed with the expert from the Prosecution a number of issues relating to different kinds of conflict. He agreed with the fact that the most difficult conflict is a conflict which occurs at home, on your own home ground. Your Honour, it was not a question of talking about occupation. If certain territories were occupied -- were occupied, it would be better to turn to the HVO and the Serbs. The Prosecution tried to underestimate the importance of this. This is important because it plays a part on the responsibility and the position of the accused. We believe that this is a relevant factor. Lastly, as far as the constitutional background is concerned, which ties into the military background, the capital city in the country, Sarajevo, was under siege. The economic power and military power were, therefore, curbed. This became an obsession for the government of this country, and this, thereby, exerting a lot of pressure on the accused; he was to find the necessary measures to free Sarajevo. He was not alone in achieving this. But this was an essential goal for the government at the time. The military background -- as I have told you, the capital city was under siege. The Territorial Defence was not ready or not prepared for war. An army was set up with all the pitfalls and difficulties one can imagine. The army needed, as can be stated in the documents we will adduce, the army was to replace the Territorial Defence. Changes were also made in the Territorial Defence, but this shift was not done overnight. This is a process which lasted over a year. And during the Defence case, we shall show how the Territorial Defence was turned into the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, and what kind of relationship existed between the two, what communication systems and what superior-to-subordinate relationship theres were, what kind of links there were between the army and the civil bodies, between the army and the Territorial Defence. We shall also, Your Honour, talk about mobilisation or call-up, and all the problems relating to the All People's Defence system. We shall also discuss what the particular assignment of the accused was. His assignment had nothing to do with the setting up of the 3rd Corps. The assignment allotted to General Hadzihasanovic was to go onsite and take control of the existing units, brigades, according to the information received from Sarajevo, that were on the spot. General Hadzihasanovic came to Zenica. He met the person who was going to become his deputy, General Merdan. The latter was the commander of the military district of the territorial force in Zenica. He had received instructions and had been asked to set up a 3rd Corps with its units and brigades. We shall explain in the course of the Defence case in which way, having seen that he could not fulfil his assignment, in which way the General Hadzihasanovic realised that his assignment got -- was changed, and he was asked to set up of the 3rd Corps. He was asked to make sure that the front line on the border with the Serb forces be maintained. And lastly, whenever possible, he was asked to bring in enough men to free the capital city Sarajevo. We shall talk about the first attempt -- in fact, it was not the first attempt, but the first attempt after the arrival of General Hadzihasanovic in Zenica. The first military operation conducted by the latter which was an attempt to free the capital city, but this failed. The witnesses and the military experts will talk about the alliance or the artificial alliance between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Witnesses will talk to you about the fact that at the time General Hadzihasanovic arrived in Zenica, there had already been problems between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, there had been clashes. The expert -- the military expert and other witnesses will talk about all the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic to prevent a conflict between these two entities. Why? Because he was a responsible commander, and he knew that if he were to set up a second front inside his area of responsibility, that this would be doomed. This area of responsibility, Your Honour, was a very large area of responsibility. It ran from the north, Maglaj; to the west, Gornji Vakuf; to the south, Visoko; just about reaching Sarajevo and to the east in Vares. There were something like 400 and 500 kilometres of front line with the Serb forces. In other words, the front line, Your Honour, was about as long as the distance from The Hague to Paris. You need a number of soldiers to fill the front line when it is that long. You need a lot of resources. And it was essential for General Hadzihasanovic to be in contact with the HVO and prevent other territories being occupied by the Serb forces. It is important to mention that in the Blaskic case, the Prosecution described the territory covered by Bosnia-Herzegovina as a very large territory. In the current case, in the opening statement of the Prosecution, we talked about a small territory, not a very large one. However, the same Prosecution in two different cases with two different objectives. I could go on and talk about shortage of resources, shortage of qualified personnel, shortage of weapons, shortage of -- or difficulty of dealing with the HVO, who became -- who turned out to be an enemy. They were to have a common enemy i.e., the Serb forces. It turned out to be different. A number of factors have an impact on command and control. What you see here on your screen are those factors which had been mentioned by the Defence team when it tried to have a number of facts admitted which had been admitted in other cases. The Prosecution had then objected and stated that these facts had nothing to do with the responsibility of the accused, as related to his duty which was to take necessary and reasonable measures. The state of preparation, resources, and sufficient weapons is something which would be addressed by the military expert. These are important criteria which have an impact on everyday life, on command and control, on how attacks on the enemy forces -- which means that the commander, as the military expert will tell you, the commander has to sometimes change his plan. He has to allocate resources where he hadn't initially intended to allocate them. And as the commander takes all of these decisions, this may change his priority. His first and foremost objective is to fulfil his assignment. The commander has to think about everything all at once. This is what the military expert will tell you. A commander who, like in the present case, is confronted with an ultimatum at the end of January 1993 at Busovaca, Novi Travnik, and Gornji Vakuf all at once is something which will change the priorities of a corps commander in a very significant manner. Another factor with I addressed a little earlier on was the HVO. The HVO was supposed to be an ally. We had already asked the HVO in December 1992 to take part alongside the Serb corps to the freeing of the town of Sarajevo. And this was not granted. All these factors combined will be set against a backdrop of the military context. The military expert will address these issues, but other witnesses that have experienced some of these events will also address these issues. And I hope, Your Honours, that you understand how these factors can have an impact on the way in which a commander runs his operations. The sixth point of my opening statement deals with the witnesses that will be called by the Defence. Who are these witnesses and what will they talk about? I've already had the opportunity to talk to you about some topics which will be addressed by these witnesses. As we mentioned earlier on, we shall call 70 witnesses, and there might be a few additional witnesses we shall add to this list. Of course, Your Honour, it is important to understand that these witnesses will not come to confirm the Prosecution's statements. But if these witnesses talk about facts which are different from those presented by the Prosecution witnesses does not mean that the witnesses are not telling the truth. These witnesses will come and give their version of the facts. It will not be a smokescreen, but this will be the truth, Your Honour. We have called a number of military experts. At the pre-trial hearing, the Trial Chamber informed us that it would be useful to let the military expert witnesses know that after having taken the solemn declaration, they no longer belong to the Defence team but belonged to the Judges. We hadn't quite understood what this meant. We didn't understand what the Trial Chamber was conveying to us at this point. What we can say, Your Honour, is that these witnesses -- and we agree that these witnesses belong to justice and that they can be cross-examined by the Prosecution. And we hope they will be cross-examined by the Prosecution so that the Trial Chamber can fully benefit from their testimony. As I have mentioned, we shall also call international witnesses who will come and testify here. These are military experts, people who were part of the British Battalion, witnesses who were members of the ECMM, and witnesses from a number of international organisations. I would like to seize this opportunity, Your Honour, to inform you of the fact that we shall have to turn to the Trial Chamber in order to obtain orders and send subpoenas out to a number of witnesses working for international organisations, or to ask international organisations to produce a number of documents. We shall file these motions in the next few days. Lastly, Your Honour, I should like to talk about the question of expert witnesses. I should briefly like to tell you what these witnesses are going to talk about. I should like to first of all talk about the constitutional expert. He will talk to you about the way the state was dismantled: the constitutional system before the war was declared, the constitutional system after the war was declared, how the governmental bodies operated during the war, and how all of this had an impact on the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. As far as the military expert is concerned, in addition to the topics I have already addressed, he will talk about the command chain, Your Honour. This is an essential item to be taken into consideration in this case. When dealing with an army corps, an army corps has a chain of command that goes right down to its lowest level, i.e., a platoon commander. When the time comes to take measures relating to a particular fact, whether it be a military operation or to prevent or to punish, the primary responsibility is, of course, to be there at the time a violation takes place. In other words, you cannot expect a corps commander who has more than 30.000 men under his control, you can't expect a commander to do everything himself. He has a chain of command. He needs to use it. And he is entitled to understand what is happening along this chain of command. I can draw a parallel here. I was talking about the Renault model. Renault is a very large company. It is quite clear, Your Honour, that if the Formula 1 Renault team in China is taking part in a race and that a crime is committed, a theft is committed by one of the teams of Renault in China, you cannot ask the CEO of the company to be the first man to be informed and to be the man who takes the necessary measures. Mr. President, it is obvious that this is a model which is quite different from the models we have in military situations, but we believe that it is a good example to give you an idea of the scale in question. The corps commander followed operational developments, followed what was done by brigades and by units. This is an important issue that should be underlined in these proceedings. There are also various levels of operation, Mr. President. And this is a matter that we will discuss with -- this is a matter that we discussed with the expert witness of the Prosecution when we asked him questions about the tactical level and the operational level and the strategic level on the basis of the posts occupied, on the basis of the level occupied, the functions of an officer are not the same. His responsibilities are not the same. And this is something that the Trial Chamber must take into consideration. The role of a corps commander, in our opinion, and the level of command is an issue that is very relevant in this case. We have a fourth expert witness, Mr. President, who will address the matter of command and control. And I would like to take the opportunity to inform you that the military expert is an expert from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he held the post of commander of the BH Army 1st Corps at about the same time that General Hadzihasanovic held his position. The person in question is General Karavelic. I would also like to tell you that I'm mentioning this issue because this witness is someone who will inform the Trial Chamber about the notion of the zone of responsibility and about links that exist between units, to inform the Chamber about a notion such as operational command, operational control, and tactical control. And he will also address the issue of administrative support. This former officer was a member of a number of armies in different countries, and he will be in a position, and this is what we believe, Mr. President, he will be in a position to inform the Trial Chamber about the possibility of seeing that there are independent units that exist and function outside the control of the forces involved in the conflict, in spite of the fact that they're located within the same theatre of operations. He will testify this is quite natural in the course of an armed conflict. I will now move on to the subject of the mujahedin, Mr. President. This is an issue which gives rise to much emotion. Who are the mujahedin? Defence counsel can certainly not deny that there were people present there. There were people who were in Central Bosnia in 1993 whom we could call the mujahedin. Nevertheless, how many of them were present there? There are witnesses who will testify about this, and you have already heard a number of witnesses, and it was claimed that it was not possible to know exactly how many such people there were. The fact that HVO propaganda existed -- and witnesses will testify about this -- this was propaganda which had an adverse effect on them, they used the mujahedin for propaganda purposes in order to portray the BH Army in a negative light. They also used the mujahedin factor in order to force their own population to abandon certain areas. But at the same time, they strived to create a myth for all the people present in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The mujahedin, Mr. President, weren't under single command. It wasn't an armed force. These people came from a number of countries, from European countries or from other countries. Witnesses will also testify about all the measures taken by the accused in order to try and deal with this problem, the effect of which was more negative within the 3rd Corps. It did more harm than good. How could one think that the 3rd Corps, that did everything in order to prevent a conflict from breaking out with the HVO, how could one think that such a corps wanted to use the mujahedin in operations? These two factors quite simply don't go together. This would have been contrary to the strategy pursued by the government. The government's strategy was to have a multi-ethnic country. This would be contrary to all the evidence that you have heard and it will be contrary to all the evidence that you will hear in the course of the Defence case. One of the witnesses whose name appears on the screen before you, is one who -- is a witness who drafted the plan for forming this notorious unit called El Mujahed. Witnesses will explain in greater detail where these people came from. They will explain what they did, and they will testify what the 3rd Corps attempted to do in order to deal with the problem. And finally, evidence will be presented to show that the attempt to create the El Mujahed unit failed. Unfortunately, the incomplete theory by the Prosecution, which was based on international witnesses who did not see or meet the mujahedin, renders the situation somewhat more difficult. On the 11th of September 2001 -- I apologise. On the 11th of September 2002, something tragic happened in New York. Since that time, the world has a better understanding of the issue of terrorism, of the issue of the mujahedin. It has a better understanding of people who belong to no country in particular and whose ideas oppose all the ideas that states have. The world has a better understanding today of the danger that such people represent. Nevertheless, we do not yet understand the phenomenon of the mujahedin; but we have a better understanding today of all the complex issues that are a result of this phenomenon. It would be illusory to believe that the situation was any different in 1993. On the contrary, these people were present in the field and someone allowed these people to enter Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nevertheless, one should not leap to the conclusion that because there were people who were present in the field - and this has been demonstrated by the evidence - these people tried to influence the local people. They tried to buy the loyalty of the local people. They had links to religion. They tried to use their money to buy local people. But it would be leaping to conclusions if one said that these people were linked to the BH Army. The witnesses who appear before you will come to explain this phenomenon to you. They will explain to you how this cohabitation - if we can use the term, because they were in Bosnia - they will explain to you how it was possible for such cohabitation to exist. But the witnesses who appear before the Chamber, Mr. President, will explain how people who were very close to senior officers in the BH Army were not only not loved, they will explain that they weren't even good soldiers and they will explain that they were problematic, and this was a situation that had to be dealt with in Central Bosnia in 1993. Naturally, this case has to do with that year, 1993. But the fact that in 1994 the problem still had not been resolved is also a factor that confirms that these people had no links to the army. And General Hadzihasanovic, the accused, shouldn't pay for what the mujahedin did and shouldn't pay for what happened on the 11th of September simply because he was in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the same time as people whom one calls mujahedin were present there. I am coming to the end of my opening statement, Mr. President, and I would like to address the issue of applicable law. In the essential elements of command responsibility, ones that have been discussed, we've discussed at the beginning the relationship between superior and subordination; we discussed whether the commander knew or had reason to know about crimes committed; and we discussed the matter of measures that were necessary or reasonable to take. As far as the superior-subordinate relationship is concerned, Mr. President, we will discuss the matter of areas of responsibility, and this is an issue that has nothing to do with the issue of the superior-subordinate relationship. Perhaps we have not understood the Trial Chamber's decision in regard to the motion for acquittal. This is an important issue that has already been dealt with, in our opinion, and we believe it is an issue that has been debated in other proceedings as well. The second question, Mr. President, the relationship of the superior and subordinates, and analysis of this matter in the Blaskic case. In this case, the Trial Chamber mentioned the necessary analysis that had to be carried out to show whether a commander had effective control over his forces, over armed forces. The expert witness, just like other witnesses, will appear to explain that this idea of superior and subordinate relationship had nothing to do with the idea of areas of responsibility or zones of control. As far as the issue of knowing or having reason to know is concerned, in the Blaskic -- the Blaskic Chamber pointed out that this concerns real information that a commander should dispose of. The Appeals Chamber also established that it could not be a matter of assumptions. And above all, it was established that a commander could not be held responsible for not having tried to obtain information. And finally, as far as the issue of measures is concerned, there's the issue of standards or of the level of caution demanded, and reference the standard we suggest the Trial Chamber should use. On a number of occasions in the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, the issue of obliging a commander to take immediate measures was addressed. And this question, the issue of taking measures immediately, if I can put it this way, the question of immediacy is one which is defined in different manners depending on the context. The expert witness for the Prosecution discussed this. Our witnesses will do the same. A few legal issues: Very briefly, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber about testimony that concerns opinions. This was an issue raised in the course of the Prosecution case. The Trial Chamber has decided to accept testimony based on witnesses' opinions. This is an issue that might make the Chamber's task more difficult. At least, this was what we argued at the beginning of the case. Nevertheless, the witnesses that we call will also come here to express their opinions, when this is relevant. As far as circumstantial evidence is concerned, it is important to us, Mr. President, to point out that circumstantial evidence must take into account all the evidence in regard to certain fact before any conclusions can be drawn. I'm referring to the inferences that one can make on the basis of evidence. This would be the English term. And it is our opinion, with all due respect, Mr. President, that before drawing any inferences from circumstantial evidence, it is necessary to take into consideration all the evidence in existence with regard to any given fact. As far as the question of armed conflict is concerned, the Trial Chamber decided not to rule on this question. The Defence will attempt to present a Defence case which takes into consideration both possibilities. Finally, there are imprecisions in counts, 5, 6, and 7. Mr. President, when the Defence raises such an issue, this is a legal issue. It does not have to do with the ultimate means of defence. The Trial Chamber noted that we have all the evidence that concerns counts 5, 6, and 7, and the evidence already shows that the accused took all the measures necessary in relation to what is contained under counts 5, 6, and 7. But we believe that when the Prosecution did not comply with its duties to be more specific in regard to these counts, we believe that it's therefore our possibility to point the fact out and to leave if to the Trial Chamber to decide about the degree of precision that should be required of the Prosecution in this case. This is not a technical issue; it is a question that is in the interests of justice. It is in the interest of -- it is in the interest of justice and it will be of benefit for the final judgement. I will now address the issues contained in the last part of my opening statement, and this explains in relation to each count, what the Defence wants to demonstrate when calling its witnesses with regard to each particular count. I suggest that we have a break now, and I will then require about another 20 minutes to conclude Defence counsel's opening statements. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you may take the floor to commence with the ninth part of your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, Mr. President, I will now move on to the last part of Defence counsel's opening statement. This part deals with the specific manner in which we intend to present evidence pertaining to the counts in the indictment; first of all, as far as Count 1 is concerned, this count concerns Dusina. The Trial Chamber in its decision on the motion for acquittal decided that there was evidence -- to draw the conclusion that the crimes committed in Dusina were committed by men who were under the control of the accused. This took place on the 26th of January 1993. And it allowed one to conclude that the accused knew, had reason to know that these crimes had been committed, and nevertheless no measures were taken. Very briefly, Mr. President, we could inform you of the fact that in the eyes of the Defence, this is an event of much importance. It is a strictly military affair, at least that's how it appears in the light of the evidence presented. But to conclude on this basis that the perpetrators of the crime were under the control of the accused is something that will be commented by on the witnesses. They will testify that there are certain doubts about the perpetrators who committed the crimes. But I'd like to deal more with the question of knowledge, Mr. President, and by addressing the matter of the meeting that was held and at which Colonel Blaskic -- Mr. Blaskic attended the meeting, and the Prosecution drew the conclusion that the accused had knowledge of the events of the 26th of January 1993. We will explain the context within which this meeting was held, and witnesses will come to explain what happened at the meeting. They will say who was present at the meeting and in what manner the information was relayed by Colonel Blaskic on this occasion. And on this basis we'll claim that the accused didn't have any knowledge. Nevertheless, Mr. President, the Defence believes that measures were taken with regard to Dusina. An investigation was conducted, and witnesses will come to testify about this before the Trial Chamber in the course of the Defence case. As I said earlier on, the importance of this event is that no mujahedin were involved in this event, and this will enable the Defence to underline the measures taken by the accused in such a situation and just as the accused took measures in connection with other situations which are already in evidence. As far as the count concerning Miletici is concerned, we will show that these crimes were committed by people who were not under the control of the 3rd Corps. These crimes were in this case perpetrated by the mujahedin. There are witnesses who will appear to testify how these people who were not members of the 3rd Corps committed the crimes in Miletici. As far as knowledge in the case of Miletici is concerned, as the Prosecution has already stated, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps was at the site on the day following the crimes in Miletici, and he will be in a position to explain to you in great detail the measures that were taken at the time, in spite of the fact that, according to the Tribunal's jurisprudence, it was not his responsibility to take any steps or measures at that time. As far as the issue of Maline is concerned, the crimes that were committed in June, witnesses will appear to testify about the crimes covered by Count 1, and they will testify that these crimes were perpetrated by people who were not members of the 3rd Corps. The men who were killed on that day were killed by the mujahedin, and they included masked, local people. But all these people were not under the control of the 3rd Corps. The witness will explain exactly how groups were separated on that day. We will hear explanations about how the people who were killed on that day were literally kidnapped, taken from the hands of the BH Army, and they were then taken to a place where they were executed. Evidence has already demonstrated that certain measures were taken, and witnesses will come to provide additional explanations about when people who were members of the 3rd Corps first came to know about these crimes. And they will come to testify about the measures they took at that time. As far as count 3 is concerned and with regard to Orasac, the Trial Chamber drew the conclusion that there was evidence allowing one to draw the conclusion that the people who had committed murder by ritual beheading were under the control of the 3rd Corps and that the accused knew or had reason to know about this and nevertheless failed to take any measures. The Defence will have recourse to a certain number of documents and a certain number of witnesses to contest these three crimes. First of all, the people who committed the crime in Orasac were mujahedin who weren't under the 3rd Corps and were in no way were they members of the 3rd Corps. They had no links with the 3rd Corps. As far as knowledge is concerned, he had absolutely no knowledge of these events. If people within the 3rd Corps, and this doesn't involve the accused, if they had any knowledge of the crimes in Orasac, they had knowledge of the kidnapping and legal detention. This is the only kind of knowledge they might have had, but they never had any knowledge about the crimes that were committed in Orasac. In addition, a number of measures were taken, and witnesses will appear before the court to explain to you, Mr. President, how everyone was attempting to discover what exactly happened in Orasac, whether it's the BritBat or the International Committee of the Red Cross, or the EC Monitoring Mission, or members of the operational groups, member of the Bosanska Krajina Operational Group. All these groups took measures to try and determine what exactly happened in Orasac. As far as Count 3 is concerned and as far as the situation involving a detainee known as Havranek is concerned, the Defence counsel will show that the accused had no knowledge of these events. Nevertheless, measures were taken; measures were taken by a subordinate of the accused without the accused being aware of them. And as far as Count 3 is concerned and the murder at Zrno, it is our respectful submission that it has already been proved that this person wasn't killed by people under the 3rd Corps. These persons were not killed by 3rd Corps members. We will also deal with the issue of knowledge and the measures taken after this crime was committed. As far as Count 4 is concerned, and more specifically as far as the music school is concerned, the Defence will strive to demonstrate that measures were taken once the accused had been informed that crimes may have been committed in the music school. We will demonstrate that under the circumstances that prevailed at the time, the accused did take certain steps. As far as the music school is concerned, Mr. President, witnesses will come to testify that the events don't have the scope claimed by the Prosecution. Contrary to what the Prosecution claims, not everyone knew what was happening in the music school. As far as the crimes in Travnik are concerned, witnesses will come to show that there was no knowledge of these events, and documents will be provided to support this claim. As far as Mehurici is concerned under Count 4, the crimes that took place in Mehurici should be divided into two categories. First of all Defence counsel will try to show by having recourse to its witnesses that there was no maltreatment in the Mehurici secondary school. Secondly, Mr. President, Defence counsel will prove that the accused never had any knowledge of the crimes committed in Mehurici, whether they were committed in the elementary school or in the blacksmith's shop. As far as Orasac is concerned, I'll refer to the same arguments already presented. They're also valid for Count 4. As far as the Sretno Motel is concerned, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber concluded that there were elements that might allow a reasonable jury or a reasonable judge to come to the conclusion that these crimes were committed by people who were under the effective control of the accused. And the accused could have had knowledge of these crimes, and yet measures weren't taken. In these cases, Mr. President, our Defence will be that the perpetrators of these crimes were not under the control of the 3rd Corps and the issue of knowledge of these crimes will also be contested. As far as Bugojno is concerned, Mr. President, first of all, there's the question of the bank in Bugojno. Defence counsel will demonstrate through evidence that has already been heard and through witnesses and documents that there was no maltreatment in the Bugojno bank. As far as other detention centres are concerned, each of these locations we will challenge the superior-subordinate relationship as well as the issue of knowledge and the measures undertaken by subordinates of the commander without him knowing it. As far as Count 5 is concerned and destruction, as we have already heard during the Prosecution case, the Defence wishes to demonstrate that there has been no destruction, or not enough to render this destruction a violation of international law. There has been no destruction of towns and villages, as it has been stated. Your Honour, we will also demonstrate that the evidence adduced by the Prosecution, we will demonstrate that the Prosecution witnesses which -- who state that they saw these areas being destroyed, they could not see the destruction and what they reported is insufficient grounds to allege such a crime. Also, we can demonstrate that a number of measures were taken as regards destruction. As far as Count 6 is concerned and looting, Your Honour, we don't have the names of the people who looted the property. But we have witnesses who can state that the looting did not take place during the military operations, but after. In this case, the identity of these people is crucial. We don't know who these people were, and this is a very important element. However, we do have evidence, and evidence we will adduce pertaining to the number of measures taken by the accused against people who committed these offences to prevent these offences taking place. Lastly, Your Honour, as far as Count 7 is concerned, i.e., destruction of institutions dedicated to religion, there has been no destruction in Guca Gora nor in the Jean Baptiste Church in Travnik. These people had no connection with the 3rd Corps. It has already been demonstrated and will be further demonstrated during the Defence case. In the same way, Your Honour, a number of measures were taken without looking into the facts that these acts were committed by people who had no connection with the 3rd Corps. Going well and beyond the responsibility, the subordinates of the accused took the necessary measures despite this to make sure that the damages be repaired and that the offenders be punished. Your Honour, very briefly, this is in essence the evidence that will be adduced in the course of this trial. More importantly, the issue of measures comes up again and again. In its response to the motion filed by the Prosecution for acquittal, the Prosecution has asked to reverse the burden of the proof. This burden of proof has been denied by the Trial Chamber and has confirmed that the Prosecution had to prove whether one way or another that it is the -- this rests on the Prosecution to clearly demonstrate that the necessary measures were not taken. Conversely, we would like to show that the measures were taken, the necessary measures were taken contrary to what the Prosecution has stated. However, Your Honour, we will call a number of witnesses who will explain to what extent the subordinates of the accused were prepared, or measures that were prepared to do to prevent such offences from occurring and were prepared to punish people who were about to commit these offences. When these people came under the control of the 3rd Corps, in very special cases -- in a particular case, we may explain that the 3rd Corps -- or even if these men committing these offences were not under of the control of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic, the responsibility of the subordinates was also taken into account, and they took all the necessary measures to prevent this from happening. I shall now reach my conclusion, Your Honour, conclusion I shall make at the end of my opening statement. I should like to remind the Trial Chamber that in the name of General Hadzihasanovic, at the time we wish to adduce evidence, it is important to assess the charges in a global context. These charges cannot be considered in an isolated manner. We cannot perceive these as being isolated incidents with no connection with one another. It is the overall situation in Bosnia in 1993 that needs to be looked into. It is the overall military context which needs to be addressed in which the accused -- which the accused faced; also the fact that the accused took a number of measures to prevent these offences from taking place and preventing those men under his control in the 3rd Corps from committing such offences. The Defence respectfully submits, Your Honour, how important it is to not lose sight of the objective in this case, the objective of command responsibility in this particular case. This is what the whole case hinges on. The commander Hadzihasanovic: Did he behave in a responsible manner or not? Did he move away from the common standard, which would mean that he behaved like a criminal? The Defence respectfully submits that the evidence adduced so far demonstrates the contrary. And the additional evidence that the Defence will present will confirm this. Lastly, Your Honour, the question we need to ask ourselves at the end of the trial is not to know whether General Hadzihasanovic should be sentenced or convicted. If another commander had been in General Hadzihasanovic's shoes, how many additional crimes would have been committed in Central Bosnia? This officer commanded in an impossible situation and was able to prevent crimes from being committed on a much larger scale. The accused was able to set up and train his men in the 3rd Corps and save the situation in Central Bosnia and make sure that this army which had been set up from scratch was turned into a professional army which was able to be deployed in the country over the next few years. As also, we have to put this to the test and compare it with the Yamashita trial. I quoted some exerts from the Yamashita trial. The Yamashita case is something quite specific. We need to remember that in this particular case, the only real trial involving command responsibility, there were 123 offences that had been alleged which came under the one and single count that this person was tried for. In other words, he had not fulfilled his job as a commander. 153 offences had been committed by his subordinates. More than 25.000 victims as a result of it, in the Philippines. And a superior-subordinate relationship had been established between the perpetrators of these acts and General Yamashita. And the total failure by this commander to take the necessary measures in these circumstances. And this officer was a military governor, and in this case the area of responsibility took on a particular legal importance. General Hadzihasanovic's case is quite different. General Yamashita was proved guilty. Your Honour, when we look into the Yamashita case which was heard before the Appeals Chamber of the supreme Court of the United States, I strongly recommend the Trial Chamber read the opinion of the judges in this case. The dissenting opinion put forward by the judges did clearly talk about the miscarriage of justice in this particular trial pertaining to the facts I have just mentioned. In the first trial, in the very first trial where command responsibility was [as interpreted] an issue before the International Tribunal, we don't want this to be repeated again. The case law of the International Tribunal has been clearly spelled out when it comes to providing various evidence material, and we are convinced that the evidence material adduced by the Defence will convince the Trial Chamber that General Hadzihasanovic should not be tried before this Tribunal. Your Honour, the facts adduced as evidence are totally different to what has been presented by the Prosecution for all the measures taken are contrary or stand counter to the fact the person in question would have omitted to take the necessary measures. Also, the proof of morality of General Hadzihasanovic. This evidence stands counter to the evidence presented by the Prosecution. How can anybody with such qualities, things which people still corroborate, how could anybody who has taken such measures, how could anybody of this kind omit to take any necessary measures? This stands counter to the evidence already adduced in this case. Lastly, Your Honour, I would just like to finish off by saying that the issue of international criminal law and beyond all reasonable doubt issue needs to be addressed here. Some people believed or some people try to convince me that beyond any reasonable doubt is not a criterion which suffices and that the accused must prove his innocence. I don't agree with this. I trust in the international legal system, and I am sure that at the end of this trial, once you will have heard and seen the documentary evidence and the testimony which the Defence will adduce, that if there were still a doubt in the minds of the Judges of this Trial Chamber as regards responsibility of General Hadzihasanovic as a commander, in light, of course, of command responsibility and criteria to be applied, I am sure the Trial Chamber will acquit General Hadzihasanovic of all the counts charged in the indictment. International criminal justice and the well-being of international criminal justice depends largely on the justice rendered. Your Honour, I would lastly talk about the completion strategy of the International Tribunal. We thought that the way in which the Defence team adduced some of the evidence during the Prosecution case, this could terminate this trial. We feel that this is not warranted, and we feel this should not be -- case should not be tried before this International Tribunal. We are prepared to fully conduct the Defence relating to each count in the indictment, and the Defence will endeavour to do this over the next few months. We shall not bear in mind the completion strategy, whether it be in June or before. The Defence team is convinced that it will be able to provide you with the -- sufficient evidence material enabling you to acquit General Hadzihasanovic for each count in the indictment. I thank you, Your Honours. I have completed my opening statement, and I shall give the floor to my colleague who will address the issue of the first witnesses who will be called into this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Before giving the floor to your colleague, I would like to read Article 84 bis, which is the opening statement has just been made pursuant to Article 84. But we also have Article 84 bis. "After the opening statements by the parties or pursuant to Article 84, the Defence decides to make its opening statement after that of the Prosecution, the accused can make a deposition if he so wishes and the Trial Chamber so decides, make a statement under the control of the Trial Chamber. The accused shall not be compelled to make a solemn declaration and shall not be examined about the content of the statement. The Trial Chamber shall decide on the probative value, if any, of the statement." The Rules of Procedure and Evidence clearly state that after an opening statement, an accused, if he so wishes, may take the floor and make a statement which doesn't give rise to any questions or to any discussion. This is something I wish to bring to your attention. You can think about it until tomorrow, unless we move on to the next stage in these proceedings and unless you wish to talk about tomorrow's witness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has already taken a stance on this matter. When the Prosecution made its opening statement, we at that time opted for the following, after having discussed it with General Hadzihasanovic, that he would not make a statement. This time, we have also discussed this with General Hadzihasanovic, and he will not make a statement. However, the question of the testimony of the accused is something which remains an open question. As I mentioned earlier on, this is something which we shall decide upon as the case unfolds. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Rule 84 bis does not apply, therefore, as you have stipulated that you do not wish to make use of it. I shall, therefore, give the floor to your colleague, Mrs. Edina Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we have already informed the Trial Chamber and our learned friends from the Prosecution, this week we are going to call three witnesses. The first one is Zijad Caber. The second one is Remzija Siljak, and the third witness is Hamed Mesanovic. We have also indicated in our submissions what circumstances will the witnesses talk about. Our first witness is present here today. However, Mr. President, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber, given the fact that it is very late in the day and that we would like the witness to start and finish his testimony in one day, we would like to ask the Trial Chamber to defer the testimony of this witness until tomorrow. And it is not just the time, but also the fact that we would like this witness, who was the commander of the municipal staff of Travnik and later on of one of the brigades of the 3rd Corps -- we would need a military map in the courtroom when the witness testifies, and we will be able to have that tomorrow. There is yet another reason. You know that from the very beginning, both parties in the procedure and the Trial Chamber have been faced with the problem of translation. Despite all the efforts on the part of the Defence, we have received the translations only yesterday afternoon, and we sent those documents to the Prosecution earlier today. The OTP have informed us that due to the number of documents, that they will object to the documents being shown to the witness before tomorrow. For all these three reasons, we would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to defer the testimony of this witness until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. At this stage, the Chamber will reach the decision tomorrow on the certification, and we are going to have first the oral decision, and then the written decision which will confirm our oral decision. We are going to resume at quarter past 2.00 tomorrow, unless the Prosecution wants to say something on any of the issues, outstanding issues at the moment? Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The only issue, and it's one that I believe is in the process of being resolved, relates to our earlier request that the Defence, in addition to providing a list of witnesses, indicates which specific exhibits they plan on tendering through that witness. My discussion at the last break with Mr. Bourgon, my learned colleague, indicates that they in fact will do so. We would certainly appreciate that with respect to the remaining witnesses for this week, as well as when they file their list for the following two weeks so that we be given notice and time to prepare with respect to which documents go with which witness. But it's my understanding that they will be taking care of that. I simply wanted to place that on the record. Thank you, Mr. President. We have nothing further for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. I am turning towards the Defence to see whether when you start your case, will you then be able to provide the Chamber with a file with all the documents, or are we going to have look for the documents based on their numbers? Can you give us an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to facilitate the work of the Trial Chamber, and also to make the witnesses' life easier, we are going to try and make an effort to present our documents in the way we did in the past. I have already prepared documents for the witness who is supposed to testify tomorrow, and we will provide the Trial Chamber and our learned friends with all these documents tomorrow. It is not our problem. Our problem does not lie in the fact that we do not want to inform the OTP of all the documents that we are preparing for a witness. Our problem lies in the fact that we cannot send the documents that have not been translated. This is why we have to wait until the very last moment to tell you what number -- what documents we can give you, because about 50 per cent of the documents from our list have not been translated yet. However, we will do our utmost to facilitate the work in this courtroom by giving the documents to the Trial Chamber and to our learned friends in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this explanation. This is going to be very useful for the Judges. Can we then draw the conclusion that when the witnesses come, we will have a file or a binder every time to accompany the testimony of such witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the witnesses who will be presented with documents, the Trial Chamber is going to be provided by binder, although these documents have already been accompanied by our list. However, we are going to have a binder of all the documents that will actually be presented to the witness. In our understanding of this fact I believe is correct [as interpreted]. Some of the witnesses will be presented with documents which have already been tendered into evidence either as Prosecution evidence or Defence evidence. We are going to use these documents, and we are going to place them in our binders. However, we believe that we do not have the obligation to indicate those documents on the list of documents that will be presented to the witness because those are the pieces of evidence that are already at the disposal of both the Prosecution and the Defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, again, for this clarification. The Judges have understood that when you present us with a binder, there will be two types of documents, documents that have already been admitted into evidence either entered by the Prosecution or yourself, and new documents. It will be very useful at this moment to make a distinction in the binder as to which type of documents are we talking about, whether it is a Prosecution document, a Defence document, or a new document that is being presented. Since we have addressed all the issues, I would like to invite you to come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of October, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
